title: Call Tracking Webhooks: What They Do and How to Use
h1: Call tracking webhooks: what they do and how to set them up
description: Call tracking webhooks send each call to your CRM or buyer system instantly. Learn how to set them up, secure them and avoid common mistakes.
faq: They are automatic messages a call platform sends to a URL you control when an event happens on a call, such as a call ending, so other systems get the data instantly.
How do I secure a call tracking webhook?
Check the signature on every incoming message, answer quickly, and ignore repeats by storing call IDs you have already processed.
Do I need webhooks for pay per call?
Not always. If you only need periodic summaries, downloadable statements are enough. Webhooks help when another system must act on each call as it happens.
body:
Call tracking webhooks are automatic messages your call platform sends to another system the moment something happens on a call, so your CRM, buyer system or spreadsheet gets the data without anyone exporting a report. If you run pay-per-call campaigns, webhooks are the simplest way to keep every system working from the same call record.

What call tracking webhooks actually do

A webhook is a small web request. You give your call platform a URL that you control. When a chosen event happens, such as a call arriving, a call ending or a recording being ready, the platform sends the details of that call to your URL. Your system receives it, reads it and acts.

The alternative is polling: your system keeps asking, "Anything new?" Polling wastes effort and is always a little late. A webhook pushes the news to you when it happens.

Why pay-per-call operators use them

  • Buyer systems stay current. A buyer's CRM can create a record as soon as a call ends, with the caller, campaign and duration attached.
  • Affiliate and publisher reporting stays in step. Your own dashboard or sheet can update per call instead of once a day.
  • Alerts fire on time. A failed or unusual call can trigger a message to your team in the tools they already use.
  • Disputes get shorter. When every party's system holds the same call record, there is less to argue about. For more on that, see our guide to automating affiliate payouts.

The data a call webhook usually carries

Exactly which fields you receive depends on your platform, so check its documentation. In general, a call event describes who called, which tracking number and campaign it hit, when it started, how long it lasted and what happened to it. Map the fields you need into your own system and ignore the rest.

How to set up a call webhook, step by step

  1. Decide the job. Write down what should happen when a call ends: create a CRM record, update a sheet, notify a buyer. One clear job per webhook is easier to debug.
  2. Build a receiving URL. It must accept a POST request and answer quickly with a success code. Do the heavy work after you reply, not before.
  3. Verify the sender. Anyone can send a request to a public URL. Check the signature on every message so you only act on genuine ones.
  4. Handle repeats. Networks fail and senders retry, so the same event can arrive twice. Store a call ID and skip anything you have already processed.
  5. Test with a real call. Place a test call and watch the message arrive before you send live traffic. Our pay per call launch checklist covers this kind of pre-launch check.
  6. Watch for failures. Decide who looks at failed deliveries and how often.

Common webhook mistakes

  • Skipping signature checks. An unsigned endpoint can be fed fake calls, which then flow into payouts.
  • Slow endpoints. If your URL takes too long, the sender may treat it as failed and retry.
  • No record of deliveries. When a buyer says "we never got that call," you need a log to answer.
  • Doing everything in one webhook. Split jobs so one failing step does not block the others.

A simple example: webhooks across a campaign

Picture a campaign with one publisher, two buyers and a team that handles payouts. When a call ends, one webhook updates the publisher's reporting sheet, another creates a record in a buyer's system, and a third posts a note to a team chat if the call was very short. Each endpoint has one job. If the buyer's system is down for an hour, the other two keep working, and the delivery log shows exactly which messages need to be sent again.

This is also why short, clear call rules matter. If a buyer only pays for calls above a minimum length, the duration in the webhook becomes the number everyone checks. Read minimum call duration rules in pay per call to see how to set that expectation up front.

Questions to ask before you build

  • Which system is the source of truth for a call: the call platform or your CRM?
  • Who owns the endpoint and who gets told when it fails?
  • How long do you keep delivery records for disputes?
  • Does a partner need their own feed, or is a portal view enough?

When a webhook is not the answer

If you only need a weekly summary, a downloadable statement is simpler than building an endpoint. Use webhooks when timing matters or when another system must act on each call.
